newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ analysts warn offshore of election implications.
newsitem.headline: NZ analysts warn offshore of election implications.

text.p: New Zealand's high real yields have continued to lure offshore funds despite Saturday's general election, but some analysts say foreign investors may be underestimating the risks.
"Perhaps there are some out there who have failed to fully understand the implications of what a change of government could mean," said one economist who declined to be named.

"Certainly from the point of view of domestic investors, there is some doubt as to whether international investors fully grasp what the implications of that would be -- the potential for fiscal slippage."

The opposition Labour Party has surged in two recent polls to within four points of the conservative National government. Labour looks set to oust National if it gains the support of nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance.

London Bond Broking Company director of research Stephen Lewis said earlier this week that this would boost New Zealand's capital markets, since he expected a Labour-led government to commit itself to tight fiscal policies.
Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London, backed Lewis, saying that even a change to a left-wing coalition would not necessarily mean looser government purse strings.
New Zealand analysts were inclined to disagree.

Roger Kerr, executive director of merchant bank Bancorp, said fiscal policy would be the largest risk factor for the markets to assimilate if the election result was a Labour-led left-of-centre coalition.
"It appears that the financial markets need reminding that the Labour Party's economic policy plan offers the largest threat to fiscal achievement," he said.
The sheer volume of capital inflows into Kiwi dollars this year -- about NZ$5 billion -- had distorted the ability of the local markets to reflect the true political risk factor.
"The timing and volumes of the capital inflows from Euro-Kiwi and Samurai issues have very little to do with our election campaign or politicians' promises," Kerr said.

"The overseas investors are blinded by the yield return and the weight of money has overwhelmed any local selling of bonds or the New Zealand dollar from people worried about the election and potential changes to economic policy."

Debt market dealers expect interest rates to rise about 25 to 30 basis points if a Labour-led government emerges from the election, and currency traders said the Kiwi would pull back. "If nearly all parties are going to raise government spending

(particularly as a percentage of GDP), and assuming the Reserve Bank Act remains intact, then the Reserve Bank will have little option but to engineer a rise in rates to counteract the inflationary pressures," said David Wolfenden, Managing Director of Countrywide Banking Corporation.
Some local market players are concerned that offshore investors appear to have misread the implications of a change of government.

"Some people are gagging that these fund managers, who presumably look after many billions of dollars worth of bonds, would make such uninformed comments about the potential for things to blow up in their faces," one economist said.
"In terms of where we go next week, it will largely be them, the international investors, that are calling the shots."
